title: Scaling and Load Balancing
summary: Add capacity without adding chaos: stateless services, smart routing, health checks, and a plan for hotspots.
keyPoints: Vertical scaling makes one machine bigger; horizontal scaling adds more machines.
Horizontal scaling is easier when services are stateless and sessions live in a shared store.
Load balancers choose a backend with round robin, least connections, or hashing.
Layer 4 balances by address and port; layer 7 routes by request content.
TLS termination centralizes certificates but moves trust to the internal network.
Health checks remove unhealthy backends, but a health check is not a full correctness test.
Consistent hashing limits reshuffling when the backend pool changes.

complexity.note: The database often becomes the limit.

complexity.time: O(keys / N) moved, not all keys
complexity.note: Adding one node moves a fraction.
More flexible and more expensive than layer 4.

commonMistakes: Scaling stateless web servers while leaving a single database as the real bottleneck.
Storing session state on one server and then enabling round robin across many.
Using a health check that passes while the service is functionally broken.
Ignoring hot keys; uniform hashing does not help if one key gets most of the traffic.
Making a single load balancer the new single point of failure.
Terminating TLS at the edge and leaving sensitive internal traffic unencrypted without saying so.
interviewNotes: Say what is stateful. The stateful parts determine how hard scaling will be.
Name the load-balancing algorithm and why it fits the workload.
Say whether the balancer is layer 4 or layer 7, and where TLS terminates.
If the design uses sticky sessions, name the failure mode when a backend dies.
For a hot key, describe a mitigation such as request coalescing, a local cache, or splitting the key.

checkYourself.question: Why are stateless services easier to scale horizontally?
checkYourself.answer: Any backend can serve any request, so the load balancer can distribute traffic freely and replace a failed instance without losing user state.

checkYourself.question: When is consistent hashing useful?
checkYourself.answer: When clients or cache keys are mapped to backends and adding a backend should not remap almost every key.

checkYourself.question: What is a hot key?
checkYourself.answer: A key that receives a disproportionate share of traffic, so the single backend responsible for it becomes overloaded even when the overall load is balanced.
